strong_form: Holding factual content constant, swapping words of different emotional valence changes audience judgments more than a comparable change in the stated facts does.
weak_form: Valence-laden synonyms reliably shift judgments and even memory while the facts stay the same.
refuted_if: Controlled experiments that vary connotation and factual content independently show the factual changes move judgments more than the connotation changes do.

prior_art.citation: Wikipedia, 'Emotive conjugation' (Russell, BBC Brains Trust 1948; linked to Luntz's wording research)
Loftus & Palmer 1974: 'smashed' vs 'hit' raised speed estimates (40.8 vs 34 mph) and false memories of broken glass

strongest_criticism: Wording effects are real but usually modest. Loftus-Palmer worked on a quantity people were already unsure of, and framing effects shrink when people know the subject or hold strong views. Nobody has directly tested the comparative claim that valence matters 'more than facts'. The device itself is old and widely known.
